attempts = 0

explanationEn: `while count > 0` prints a countdown and decrements until the condition fails, `until attempts == 2` increments until its condition becomes true, and `3.times` runs the block with indices `0` to `2`. Se elige `times` cuando se conoce la cantidad de repeticiones, y `while` o `until` cuando un valor o estado controla el ciclo.

code:
def repeat(times)
  index = 0
  while index < times
    yield index
    index += 1
  end
end

repeat(3) { |i| puts "Tick #{i}" }

repeat(2) do |i|
  puts "do-end #{i}"
end

def twice(&)
  yield
  yield
end

twice { puts "Again!" }
sourceAttribution: hand-authored for the crystal-foundations-v1 Learning Route
tldrEn: `yield` calls the caller's block; `&` declares a block parameter
tldrEs: `yield` llama al bloque de quien invoca; `&` declara el parámetro de bloque
explanationEn: `repeat` yields each index to the block the caller passes, first with a brace block and then with a `do`/`end` block, and `twice` declares its block with `&` and calls `yield` twice. `yield` runs whatever block the method received, `def twice(&)` declares that block parameter explicitly so the method expects one, and the brace and `do`/`end` forms pass the same kind of block. This pattern writes an algorithm once and lets callers inject the per-item behavior.
explanationEs: `repeat` entrega cada índice al bloque que pasa quien llama, primero con llaves y luego con `do`/`end`, y `twice` declara su bloque con `&` y llama a `yield` dos veces. `yield` ejecuta el bloque que recibió el método, `def twice(&)` declara ese parámetro de bloque de forma explícita para que el método espere uno, y las formas con llaves y con `do`/`end` pasan el mismo tipo de bloque. Este patrón permite escribir un algoritmo una vez y dejar que quien llama inyecte el comportamiento por elemento.

  users[name]?
end

users = {"ada" => "Ada Lovelace"}

name = find_user(users, "ada")
if name
  puts name.upcase
end

missing = find_user(users, "grace")
puts missing.inspect
puts missing.try(&.upcase).inspect
puts missing || "Unknown"

titleEs: Seguridad ante nil y tipos unión
tldrEn: `[]?` returns `nil` for missing keys; `if` narrows the type
tldrEs: `[]?` devuelve `nil` si falta la clave; `if` estrecha el tipo
explanationEn: `find_user` uses `users[name]?`, so a hit returns the stored string and a miss returns `nil`; the `if name` branch can call `upcase`, and the missing case prints `nil` twice before falling back to `"Unknown"`. `users[name]?` has type `String?`, shorthand for `String | Nil`, and `if name` narrows it to `String` inside the branch, while `try(&.upcase)` calls the method only when the receiver is not nil. This is how Crystal pushes you to handle absence explicitly instead of crashing on a missing key, and `||` supplies the final fallback.
explanationEs: `find_user` usa `users[name]?`, así que un acierto devuelve el string guardado y una ausencia devuelve `nil`; la rama `if name` puede llamar a `upcase`, y el caso faltante imprime `nil` dos veces antes de caer en `"Unknown"`. `users[name]?` tiene tipo `String?`, abreviatura de `String | Nil`, e `if name` lo estrecha a `String` dentro de la rama, mientras que `try(&.upcase)` llama al método solo si el receptor no es nil. Así Crystal obliga a manejar la ausencia de forma explícita en vez de fallar por una clave faltante, y `||` aporta el respaldo final.

def linear_search(items : Array(Int32), target : Int32) : Int32?
  items.each_with_index do |item, index|
    return index if item == target
  end
  nil
end

explanationEn: Linear search walks the array with `each_with_index`, comparing each item against the target. The moment an item matches, `return index` exits early; if the loop finishes, the method falls through to `nil`, which is why the return type is `Int32?`. Use it on small or unsorted collections where simplicity matters more than speed: it is O(n) and needs no ordering.

Se usa en colecciones pequeñas o sin ordenar, donde la simplicidad pesa más que la velocidad: es O(n) y no requiere ningún orden previo.

def binary_search(items : Array(Int32), target : Int32) : Int32?
  low = 0
  high = items.size - 1

  while low <= high
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if items[mid] == target
      return mid
    elsif items[mid] < target
      low = mid + 1
    else
      high = mid - 1
    end
  end

  nil
end
sourceAttribution: hand-authored for the crystal-algorithms-v1 Learning Route
tldrEn: Halves a sorted range until the target index is found or `nil`
tldrEs: Parte el rango ordenado a la mitad hasta hallar el índice o `nil`
explanationEn: Binary search keeps a `low` and `high` boundary and shrinks the sorted range in half on every iteration. The midpoint uses `//` for floor integer division, since `/` on integers returns `Float64` in Crystal, and the half that cannot contain the target is discarded each time. def bubble_sort(items : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  sorted = items.dup
  (sorted.size - 1).times do |i|
    (sorted.size - 1 - i).times do |j|
      if sorted[j] > sorted[j + 1]
        sorted[j], sorted[j + 1] = sorted[j + 1], sorted[j]
      end
    end
  end
  sorted
end

def selection_sort(items : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  sorted = items.dup
  sorted.size.times do |i|
    min_index = i
    ((i + 1)...sorted.size).each do |j|
      min_index = j if sorted[j] < sorted[min_index]
    end
    if min_index != i
      sorted[i], sorted[min_index] = sorted[min_index], sorted[i]
    end
  end
  sorted
end

def insertion_sort(items : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  sorted = items.dup
  (1...sorted.size).each do |i|
    current = sorted[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 && sorted[j] > current
      sorted[j + 1] = sorted[j]
      j -= 1
    end
    sorted[j + 1] = current
  end
  sorted
end

def merge_sort(items : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  return items.dup if items.size <= 1

  mid = items.size // 2
  left = merge_sort(items[0...mid])
  right = merge_sort(items[mid..])

  merge(left, right)
end

def merge(left : Array(Int32), right : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  result = [] of Int32
  i = 0
  j = 0

  while i < left.size && j < right.size
    if left[i] <= right[j]
      result << left[i]
      i += 1
    else
      result << right[j]
      j += 1
    end
  end

  result.concat(left[i..])
  result.concat(right[j..])
  result
end

def heap_sort(items : Array(Int32)) : Array(Int32)
  sorted = items.dup
  n = sorted.size

  (n // 2 - 1).downto(0) { |i| sift_down(sorted, i, n) }

  (n - 1).downto(1) do |end_index|
    sorted[0], sorted[end_index] = sorted[end_index], sorted[0]
    sift_down(sorted, 0, end_index)
  end

  sorted
end

def sift_down(items : Array(Int32), root : Int32, size : Int32) : Nil
  loop do
    largest = root
    left = 2 * root + 1
    right = 2 * root + 2

    largest = left if left < size && items[left] > items[largest]
    largest = right if right < size && items[right] > items[largest]

    break if largest == root

    items[root], items[largest] = items[largest], items[root]
    root = largest
  end
end

def bfs(graph : Graph, start : String) : Array(String)
  visited = Set(String).new([start])
  queue = Deque(String).new([start])
  order = [] of String

  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node

    if neighbors = graph.edges[node]?
      neighbors.each do |neighbor|
        next if visited.includes?(neighbor)
        visited << neighbor
        queue << neighbor
      end
    end
  end

  order
end

This level-by-level traversal runs in O(V + E) and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, which is why it is the default choice for that problem.

Por cada vecino que no está en el `Set`, lo marca como visitado y lo encola, mientras que `graph.edges[node]?` devuelve `nil` sin lanzar error cuando un nodo no tiene entrada. Este recorrido nivel por nivel corre en O(V + E) y encuentra caminos más cortos en grafos sin pesos, por eso es la opción por defecto para ese problema.

def dfs(graph : Graph, node : String, visited = Set(String).new, order = [] of String) : Array(String)
  return order if visited.includes?(node)

  visited << node
  order << node

  if neighbors = graph.edges[node]?
    neighbors.each do |neighbor|
      dfs(graph, neighbor, visited, order)
    end
  end

  order
end

code:
class WeightedGraph
  getter edges : Hash(String, Array(Tuple(String, Int32)))

  def initialize
    @edges = Hash(String, Array(Tuple(String, Int32))).new
  end

  def add_edge(from : String, to : String, weight : Int32) : Nil
    (@edges[from] ||= [] of Tuple(String, Int32)) << {to, weight}
    (@edges[to] ||= [] of Tuple(String, Int32)) << {from, weight}
  end
end

def dijkstra(graph : WeightedGraph, start : String, nodes : Array(String)) : Hash(String, Int32)
  dist = Hash(String, Int32).new(Int32::MAX)
  visited = Set(String).new
  nodes.each { |node| dist[node] = Int32::MAX }
  dist[start] = 0

  while visited.size < dist.size
    current = closest_unvisited(dist, visited)
    break if current.nil?

    visited << current
    if edges = graph.edges[current]?
      edges.each do |(neighbor, weight)|
        new_dist = dist[current] + weight
        dist[neighbor] = new_dist if new_dist < dist[neighbor]
      end
    end
  end

  dist
end

def closest_unvisited(dist : Hash(String, Int32), visited : Set(String)) : String?
  best : String? = nil
  best_dist = Int32::MAX

  dist.each do |node, distance|
    if !visited.includes?(node) && distance < best_dist
      best = node
      best_dist = distance
    end
  end

  best
end
